culturalBackground: Henna has been worn across North, West and East Africa for centuries, with distinct styles in countries such as Sudan, Mali, Mauritania and Somalia.
In Sudan, henna is closely tied to weddings, and brides traditionally wear bold, dark designs on both hands and feet.
In Mali and Mauritania, artists often lay thin strips of tape on the skin and apply henna over them, which leaves crisp geometric lines when the tape is removed.
In Hausa-speaking communities of Nigeria and Niger, henna is known as lalle and is worn for weddings and festivals.
applicationTips: Bold African-style designs need a thicker line, so cut the cone tip slightly wider than you would for fine work.
For solid filled areas, apply an even layer of paste; thin patches stain lighter than the rest.
Use strips of tape or a stencil to keep long straight edges clean.

faqPool.q: What makes African henna designs different?
faqPool.a: They favour bold lines, solid fills and geometric shapes over the fine floral detail common in Indian mehndi, and the look varies a lot between regions.

faqPool.q: How is the tape technique used in West African henna?
faqPool.a: Thin strips of tape are placed on the skin in a pattern, henna is applied over the whole area, and the tape is removed after the paste dries to reveal sharp unstained lines.

faqPool.q: Is African henna only worn at weddings?
faqPool.a: No. It is also worn for Eid, naming ceremonies and other family celebrations, usually in simpler designs than bridal henna.
